title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as a Savings Account
dek: The housing fund is not a savings account you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the public sector, is especially informative.
who: Employees who have a housing fund but aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a housing fund loan, or contributing as a flexible-employment worker; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chat about how the episode came about and where the three hosts stand can be fast-forwarded; start at 13:10, where Zhou Yi's experience of using it begins.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi set up Beijing's no-threshold monthly rental withdrawal of 2000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the housing fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai points out this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you're entitled to and use everything you can use’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautions that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine for themselves — people just keep fake books for themselves.

points.h: The housing fund is not a deposit; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yubai walks through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the housing fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as buying nor as renting; even though the new rules allow withdrawal under the heading of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you will be pursued to return the entire withdrawn amount and barred from withdrawing any housing fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you're entitled to’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate above demand deposits’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

points.h: The new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees on an owner-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the housing fund no longer serves only the single purpose of a loan to buy a home. Second, rental withdrawal used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal scope. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for housing fund loans. In addition, the management centre should reply to a withdrawal application within three days and to a loan application within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

points.h: The share of housing fund money lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of housing fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, whereas at the peak it was over 70% — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out that the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds cut sharply — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the month when the withdrawal ratio turned upward was 2023, exactly matching the retirement of the 1960s cohort.

points.h: If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing your housing fund
points.body: Yubai warns: the housing fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has several caps; at application the smallest of several standards applies, for example a minimum 20% down payment for a first or second owner-occupied home, so a 1 million yuan home cannot be financed beyond 800,000 yuan; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing your housing fund as living expenses, check your city's lending rules first. Yubai is also cautious about the buying logic of ‘the rental yield is close to the housing fund rate, you're only short a down payment’: you also have to consider depreciation, price rises and falls, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 yuan down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and rate are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The contribution base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed, above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1000 to 2400 yuan, and this money is not counted toward individual income tax, but it's a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a housing fund loan, and most do not allow a one-off catch-up payment.

points.h: In the public sector, the housing fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend back home with a public-institution post, who readily showed a screenshot of her housing fund account: the monthly credit is more than twice Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeds her savings; the friend lives at home with no rental need, so the housing fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus she has an occupational annuity, and the contribution base counts bonuses and allowances in full. Lao Qian adds: the housing fund is tax-free, and with individual pension contributions capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, the public sector simply has one more layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private unit employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, versus 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full housing fund contributions are a lens on a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the housing fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that pays the housing fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run in every respect, and won't play cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximisation the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, you take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels hard done by. Lao Qian cites Ford's pay raise on the Model T — making workers able to afford the car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone gets so many app notifications you don't look carefully — say it tells you 2000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is used up and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people keep fake books for themselves, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the housing fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can withdraw at any time, but the housing fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality lending channel, the rate is so low, yet only a bit over 30% of people took out a loan — and at the peak, what was that share? Over 70%. In just a few years.
I think a company that pays the housing fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean raising costs — it also means one person's spending, the household sector's spending, becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages; the two form a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you're entitled to and use everything you can use — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country, all of it.
